texts.orig: Walmart announced in 2023 that they will close 4 of their stores in the Chicago area due to poor performance. This announcement came without warning, shocking many residents in the Chicago area, leaving many without access to fresh and affordable food and produce. Despite rallies and petitions, Walmart ultimately stuck with their decision to leave after losing millions of dollars and never making a profit once. Being able to access fresh and local food is very important to a community, this is, however, not possible for people who live in food deserts, a place with a lack of nutritious food. Despite buying local food coming with many benefits, the prevalence of food deserts creates barriers that restrict access to any benefits of buying local food.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: pointed out that this is especially true for “people living below the poverty line tend to work multiple jobs; in addition, they may also be responsible for household errands and family care”. (qtd. In Vayner) For some people the extra distance travel is an unreasonable ask as the long distance takes up too much time. This especially impacts people living under the poverty line as the cost of fuel begins to eat up the already low incomes of these communities. It’s not just poorer communities, residents of rural communities, where many retailers have found it hard to make money, also must travel for hours on end to reach the nearest grocery store. Rhonda Price, a guest on “Southeastern Ohio Food Desert”, pointed out that due to the local grocery store closing 4 years previously, the residents of the county need to drive for one hour to buy the most basic groceries. In 2016, this all added up to around 150,000 miles travelled in terms of grocery trips. The amount of distance that would be travelled for one person is negligible, but when considering that whole communities are doing the same trip. This begins to eat away at any environmental benefits of having local food transported over a shorter distance.

texts.text: When traveling around you may have noticed stores like Dollar General and Family Dollar down every block and corner. Even in the most unlikely places where you won’t even find a Walmart or any other major big box store. A reporter from

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Amanda Pintado, noticed that in areas that have lost grocery stores, dollar stores such as Dollar General come in and supply cheap food to the area. She explains that “Dollar General—which has a location in Mount Pulaski—now has 18,000 stores nationwide… dollar-store chains, which mostly sell packaged and frozen goods, have begun to offer fresh foods in some stores” (Pintado). The issue that arises from this is that fresh food choices are not the best, fresh food is more expensive because it requires more time and labor to produce. On top of the fact that for many people, dollar stores are the only option too get food at all, people are still left without access to local food.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: One of the communities that is the most affected by food deserts are those that live under the poverty line. Vayner points out in an argument against Katherine Spriggs, a local food supporter, food deserts exist overwhelmingly in low-income areas, and studies have shown that “both poverty and race matter when it comes to having healthy food options” (qtd. in Vayner). Buying locally sourced food comes at an increased cost making it less likely for low-income families and communities to afford to buy such kinds of food. Such food is not only found in stores that are far and out of reach, even if they are close by, but the higher cost acts as another barrier also restricting access to purchasing local food creating a disconnect from source and buyer.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Gunderson was telling a story “The local grocery store, in business for more than 70 years, had just closed. That meant at least a 40-mile round trip drive just to get basic groceries.” (qtd. in “A Rural Minnesota Self-Serve”). Driving such distances to spend money will not recirculate in the rural town where buyers originate from making the community poorer and poorer. Under normal circumstances, local food” supports local economies and farmers, helping food producers maintain higher levels of profitability while making it less likely that they will need to sell parcels of farmland for commercial or residential development” (“Local Food Movement”). The problem arises when food deserts come into play, when no one can buy food because it is too expensive, or the food is too far away, local farmers do not get the support that they need to stay afloat.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: One-way rural towns are fixing this problem is that they are just opening shops of their own. Evansville, a small rural town in Minnesota, has adopted a self-serve grocery store model to solve the food desert in their town. Although the cost of running the store is high and requires lots of work to maintain shelves, the residents do enjoy the benefits of having a proper store. In a farm town named Winchester, “Great Scott! (named for the surrounding county), operates as a for-profit cooperative, financed by locals who got together in a church meeting hall last year to discuss the urgent need for a grocery store in their town” (Healy). There are towns that are opening more traditional style grocery stores. Although food deserts are a large problem for many, things are being done to address the issue.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Although the local food movement brings massive benefits to those who can access it. Food deserts act as a barrier to entry for many, whether it be the far distance to travel, or the higher cost of local food, not everyone can enjoy the benefits of buying locally. People who are living under the poverty line are most affected by this because they often must work multiple jobs just to get by, they cannot afford the higher cost of local food. For many, they will continue to rely on highly processed, industrially grown food.
